newsitem.title: USA: Further growth expected for U.S. pork exports.
newsitem.headline: Further growth expected for U.S. pork exports.

text.p: Exports should continue to be a bright spot for the U.S. pork industry, with increased sales expected to Japan and markets opening in China and South Korea, pork industry officials said.

In 10 years, the U.S. has gone from a net importer of pork to a net exporter. In 1996 the industry shipped out nearly 5.6 percent of the nation's production, according to USDA and industry data provided at the World Pork Expo here.
"We see that (export) number growing even more this year," said Karl Johnson, a Mankato, Minn. hog producer and chairman of the National Pork Producer Council's Trade Committee.
U.S. pork sales to Japan should increase because foot and mouth disease in its hog herd halted Taiwan's pork exports. But the Japanese must exhaust a large supply of frozen pork.
Increased pork sales to Japan should add $3 to $6 per hundredweight to prices U.S. producers receive for hogs, Johnson said. Exports added about $10 per head to cash hog prices in 1996, he noted.
South Korea and China are also being targeted as growth areas for pork exports.
"We are excited about the potential we have with China. We don't think they can produce all that they need," Johnson said.
Beginning July 1, South Korea should open its markets to pork imports, and Nick Giordano, NPPC assistant vice president of foreign trade, expects it to increase pork imports nearly 40 percent.
On the competitive front, pork exports from the Netherlands should decrease because of a hog cholera outbreak there, said Giordano.
"At least one million hogs have been slaughtered in the Netherlands," he said. "That means there will be less European production going out."
